name: Bouvines
summary: A village on the Marque south-east of Lille, where a single bridge on the Tournai road decided where Philip II had to fight in 1214.
overview: A village in French Flanders whose one bridge over the marshy Marque shaped the fighting of 27 July 1214.
knownFor: The bridge over the Marque that fixed where the fighting of 1214 happened

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Bouvines is a village of a few hundred people in French Flanders, on the right bank of the Marque about twelve kilometres south-east of Lille and a similar distance west of Tournai. Its place in history is a matter of ground rather than of size: the road between the two cities crossed the wet valley of the Marque here by one narrow bridge, and an army moving west had to funnel over it.

On Sunday 27 July 1214 Philip II of France turned and fought on the open ground east of that bridge rather than cross it with a pursuing coalition at his back. The Battle of Bouvines broke the alliance of Otto IV, Ferdinand of Flanders and John of England in a single afternoon, and the village has been defined by that day ever since.

contentSections.title: The ground and the bridge
paragraphs: The Marque valley at Bouvines is low, wet and peaty — peat was cut here commercially until the workings were stopped for the damage they did to the land. East of the crossing the ground opens into dry farmland with room for cavalry to form, which is precisely why a bridge that could pass men only slowly mattered so much: Philip could not put his army across it in the face of an enemy, and so he fought in front of it.

The village takes its name from the Latin for ox, and local explanation ties it to a bridge wide enough for two oxen abreast. The modern commune is small — 2.71 square kilometres and 766 inhabitants at the 2023 count — and the fields east of the village are still open ground. A spring known as the fontaine Saint-Pierre is pointed out as the place where Philip rested before the fighting; that identification is village tradition, not record.

contentSections.title: How the village remembers 1214
paragraphs: The commemoration is almost entirely the work of the nineteenth century. The historical commission of the Nord raised an obelisk on the site in 1865, and between 1880 and 1885 the parish church of Saint-Pierre was rebuilt under the mayor, Félix Dehau, on a scale out of all proportion to the village. Twenty-one stained-glass windows were then made for it between 1887 and 1906, narrating the battle around the nave; they are listed as monuments historiques, and they are what most visitors now come to see.

The village also carries a memorial that joins 1214 to 1914, the two dates set together on the same monument — a striking piece of French memory that reads the medieval victory and the Great War as one continuous story of the frontier. The eight hundredth anniversary was marked at Bouvines in 2014.
